status: Integrated first pass; preserves inherited source-critical sharh

chapters.matn:
Baghdad developed around a court and an expanding urban economy whose households, workshops, markets and places of instruction drew people from many regions. Soldiers and officials received revenue from the state, but merchants, physicians, translators, jurists and teachers also worked through private patrons, families and their own circles. The Tigris and overland routes carried provisions and texts. Paper, scribes and booksellers increased the means through which knowledge could be copied, compared and circulated.

The city's sciences were not one method subdivided into faculties by the caliph. Physicians compared Greek and Syriac learning with problems of bodily treatment; mathematicians worked with numerical and geometrical proofs; translators made decisions about language and meaning; jurists investigated reports, custom and disputed rights. Scholars sometimes worked together and sometimes disagreed about the limits of one another's methods. Public support could enable difficult work, while public power could also enforce a doctrinal position, as in the *miḥnah*.

A learned city required more than an accumulation of books and clever individuals. The apprentice needed a master, the physician a patient, the scribe a correctable copy, the disputant a competent critic and the scholar time and material provision for study. These relationships gave the city's intellectual life its recurrent form. Religious learning participated in this wider work while remaining answerable to revelation and the distinction between possessing a text and becoming capable of using it well.
chapters.sharh_add:
The relationship between knowledge and ʿumrān is mediated by special kinds of social dependence. A physician may possess a transmitted treatise without yet having clinical judgment; a translator may know two languages but lack the conceptual distinctions needed for a reliable version of Galen; a jurist may know several reports without knowing the particular facts of a contested contract. Each professional competence has an internal standard and a pedagogy. None becomes valid merely because a politically powerful patron admires it.

Dimitri Gutas's analysis of Graeco-Arabic translation and the history of Ḥunayn ibn Isḥāq's scholarly labour distinguish actual people, patrons and texts from an inflated legend of one centralized “House of Wisdom” producing all sciences. Manuscript comparison, glossing, correction and teaching are acts through which a specific community improves its grasp of a subject. The adoption of paper expanded written resources but did not make every student learned or every text reliable.

The Akbarian thesis of comprehensive human perfection must not imply that one mystic or jurist is competent in every medicine, language or administrative craft. Ibn ʿArabī's station of no station concerns the nonrestriction of spiritual realization to a determinate prophetic archetype; it is not a general licence to discard disciplinary proof. A real civilizational unity can therefore consist in properly ordered and mutually accountable expertise rather than one individual monopolizing every skill.

The *miḥnah* sharpens the normative problem: a ruler can possess the power to demand statements from scholars without thereby possessing decisive authority to determine the truth of the proposition demanded. Conversely, a scholar's religious credibility does not by itself supply competence to rule all administrative matters. Baghdad's living achievement lay in a plurality of relations among teachers, scribes, patrons, reasoners, worshippers and rulers. Whether they served truth depended on what those people actually did, not the grandeur of the city.

chapters.matn:
People seeking the Prophet's ﷺ teaching learned first from those who had heard or witnessed him. His household preserved acts that public gatherings could not easily disclose; Companions taught different reports according to what they remembered and the circumstances they had seen. As generations passed, students travelled among Madinah, Makkah, Kūfah, Baṣrah, Damascus, Egypt and later regions to hear teachers, compare wording and investigate the reliability of named transmitters.

An *isnād* related a claim about how an utterance or action had reached a learner. It did not itself replace examination of the narrator, the encounter, the wording or possible disagreement. Teachers and critics considered continuity, errors, memory and textual variations. Compilations associated with al-Bukhārī and Muslim made many reports widely available through forms of scholarly criticism, but no book could reproduce the Prophet's living presence or independently settle every question about the meaning of an action.

Transmission also involved forms of formation. A student could learn the reverence due to a source, the honesty needed to report uncertainty and the patience required to hear a teacher accurately. Women as well as men transmitted, particularly in and through scholarly households; their opportunities varied across generations. The resulting learned network preserved real aspects of the Sunnah while requiring fresh practical discernment whenever those aspects were brought to bear upon the conditions of another person's life.
chapters.sharh_add:
The Prophet's actual action, a witness's remembered account, a later transmitter's performance of that account, a written recension and a jurist's application are distinct objects. One can assess their accuracy in different ways. A hadith critic asks whether words and chains bear the signs of reliable transmission; a historian may question when the accessible account first appears; a jurist asks whether the established report has general or specific legal force; a teacher of character examines how its transmitted conduct might be cultivated. Genuine knowledge in one domain is not automatically exhaustive understanding in the others.

This is exactly why the metaphor of a disciplinary “trace” needs qualification. A sound report is not a false shadow merely because it does not preserve the entirety of the original inward state. It can be binding and sufficient for a particular judgment. But an authenticated narration of the Prophet's speech does not by itself supply all the conditions through which the speech was uttered, nor does reading the narration produce the virtue it commands.

The comparison of *Muwaṭṭaʾ* recensions illustrates this internally. Differences among students may involve wording, included isnāds or Mālik's own comments; al-Shāfiʿī's citations and later transmitted versions help locate the dispute. One needs to distinguish Ibn ʿUmar's reported *ghusl* practice from Mālik's judgment of its normative force, rather than projecting the latter back into the Prophet's time. Critical method belongs to the integrity of inheritance, not to sceptical hostility toward it.

In the Akbarian interpretation, spiritual inheritance is further differentiated into works, states and realized knowledge. The person who memorizes a hadith and the person whose conduct has been transformed through it may both inherit something real but not in an identical mode. Nor may spiritual feeling override report criticism. The enduring *isnād* therefore deserves comparison with other relationships of learning and companionship without being flattened into one single initiatic chain.

chapters.matn:
A merchant's promise, an unpaid debt, a disputed inheritance or a marriage conflict required judgments concerning particular facts and rights. As Muslim communities spread across regions, customs, documents and economic arrangements varied, while the authoritative Qurʾān and Sunnah remained central to religious judgment. Jurists gathered reports, examined their authority, distinguished cases and reasoned about circumstances not already described in an identical earlier example.

Abū Ḥanīfah's students preserved and developed forms of Iraqi legal reasoning; Mālik and his transmitters attended to reports and practice in Madinah; al-Shāfiʿī systematically examined evidentiary authority; Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal and his students gave particular emphasis to transmitted sources. Other juristic traditions, including Imāmī and Zaydī ones, developed distinctive accounts of legitimate religious authority. Later pupils and teachers established more durable schools whose inherited judgments continued to be interpreted and tested.

A legal school was neither a substitute Prophet nor merely a collection of abstract verdicts. It trained people to investigate evidence, recognize a case's relevant conditions, account for opposing claims and formulate an answer under particular constraints. That acquired competence could protect households and strangers from arbitrary judgment; it could also decay into formal affiliation or rivalry when the discipline's proper end was neglected. The growth of fiqh was one necessary mode of preserving and applying the comprehensive prophetic inheritance without exhausting that inheritance.
chapters.sharh_add:
One cannot describe the legal sciences as dispensable silhouettes of the Prophet's ﷺ spiritual whole. An authoritative text and a sound method of identifying the ruling of a real transaction can preserve genuine and publicly obligatory knowledge. But they remain partial relative to the full living act. If a judge validly decides whether a debt is owed, the verdict alone does not tell us everything about the debtor's remorse, the lender's generosity, or the spiritual insight of either. Such questions may matter morally, yet their partial invisibility does not make the legal decision unreal.

Al-Shāfiʿī's *Risāla*, different recensions of the *Muwaṭṭaʾ*, and early Ḥanafī sources supply actual, historically different arguments about testimony, report, legal inference and local practice. A late manual cannot be used as an undisturbed verbatim statement of its founder. The example of variants concerning Ibn ʿUmar washing his eyes during *ghusl* requires distinguishing observed conduct from Mālik's juristic assessment. This is not an abstract debate over “following the Sunnah”: it is an inquiry into which level of authority a report can bear.

The practical virtue cultivated through legal training is **discernment** (*taḥqīq al-manāṭ* in its later technical formulation): recognizing relevant facts, legally material differences and legitimate exceptions without equating all cases. Its growth requires teachers who correct students, disputations that test reasoning, memory of precedents, and the patience to withhold a verdict when facts are incomplete. These processes can produce *malakāt* of judgment, though mastery of law does not mechanically produce humility or sincerity.

Ibn ʿArabī's station of no station offers a metaphysical analogy for the nonrestriction of wisdom to one fixed outward mode. It does not replace the jurist's method or validate a private unveiled judgment against binding revealed law. The proper civilizational relation is reciprocal: authoritative fiqh constrains abuse of claims to spiritual privilege, while character formation asks whether the bearer of legal knowledge exercises it for truth and justice. Their unity is practical and normative, not the erasure of specialization.

chapters.matn:
Teachers and travelling students needed rooms, books, time and food. Wealthy families, rulers, merchants and other donors established *awqāf* to provide recurring support for mosques, lodgings, libraries and colleges. An endowed asset could sustain a teacher after the death of the person who set it aside; legal stipulations determined which activities and beneficiaries were supported. Institutions such as Baghdad's Niẓāmiyyah became prominent, but teaching also continued in households, mosques and less formal circles.

An endowed room did not itself create knowledge. A teacher had to understand a text, answer a question, correct a student's error and transmit habits of careful judgment. A stipend made prolonged study possible but could also turn a teaching position into a source of rivalry and prestige. The founder's intention, the manager's honesty, the scholar's competence and the student's effort could reinforce or obstruct one another.

The institutions of scholarship joined a charitable use of property to the formation of human capacities. They were not pre-existing parts of a complete university system announced in Madinah. They arose through historically specific legal forms, economies and patterns of authority, while seeking to sustain functions present in early practices of prophetic instruction. Their success depended upon what people actually learned and became, not merely upon the survival of a building, a deed or a celebrated scholarly title.
chapters.sharh_add:
The institution of *waqf* provides a particularly clear meeting of the four causes and the vertical end of knowledge. Material property and its yields support the work; founders, judges, managers and labourers contribute efficient action; the legally defined deed and recurring arrangements give the institution recognizable form; the promised support of teaching and worship names a proximate purpose. Whether the institution is actually just and conducive to the formation of truth-loving persons is a distinct normative question, not automatically answered by the existence of the deed.

The historian must trace the actual arrangement: which asset generated income, who held appointment power, who was eligible for stipends, and what was taught. Michael Chamberlain's study of Damascus prevents a picture of the madrasa as one modern bureaucratic university model. Scholarly households, patronage, personal reputation and competition for office remained essential.

The *malaka* of legal or spiritual understanding is not acquired by sitting beneath a college roof. Repetition, interpretation, correction and disciplined company are required; even those may be distorted by vanity or mere desire for certification. The Akbarian emphasis on realized knowledge can expose this difference without denying the real value of texts and stipends. The outward form can be a necessary condition for living formation, but it is not its sufficient cause.

The history therefore has two distinct continuities: material-institutional persistence and human continuity through competence. A college can persist after its leading teacher dies while its educational quality changes; a teaching lineage may survive outside an endowed building. The future of Islamic civilization depends upon both kinds, including the ways they correct and sustain one another.
